By [Author Name], CNN
Updated 11:42 AM EDT, [Date]

**(CNN) —** Los Alamos National Laboratory, the birthplace of the atomic bomb and one of the nation’s premier nuclear research facilities, has begun notifying thousands of current and former workers, contractors, and visitors that they may have been exposed to toxic beryllium dust.

The notifications, sent out in recent weeks by the Department of Energy (DOE) and laboratory management, stem from an extensive historical review of air monitoring records and contamination tracking across multiple facilities at the New Mexico complex. 

Officials say the potential exposures span several years and involve multiple buildings where beryllium—a lightweight, highly rigid metal critical to the production of nuclear weapons components—was machined, tested, or stored.

"Out of an abundance of caution, we are reaching out to individuals who worked in or visited specific technical areas where historical monitoring indicates beryllium dust may have been present above action levels," a spokesperson for the National Nuclear Security Administration (NNSA) said in a statement to CNN. "The health and safety of our workforce and our community remains our highest priority."

While beryllium is an essential element in defense manufacturing, inhaling even microscopic particles of its dust can be hazardous. Exposure can trigger a sensitizing immune response, which in some individuals develops into Chronic Beryllium Disease (CBD)—an incurable, debilitating lung condition characterized by scarring, shortness of breath, fatigue, and an increased risk of lung cancer. 

Crucially, symptoms of beryllium disease can take anywhere from a few months to several decades to manifest after initial exposure.

### A growing net of notifications

The sheer scale of the outreach has raised concerns among worker advocacy groups and local community members. The laboratory, which employs more than 14,000 people, hosts hundreds of external researchers, sub-contractors, and official visitors every year. 

According to officials, the letters advise recipients of their potential exposure dates, the specific facilities involved, and instructions on how to access free medical screening. The screening primarily involves a specialized blood test—the Beryllium Lymphocyte Proliferation Test (BeLPT)—which determines whether an individual's immune system has become sensitized to the metal.

"Receiving a letter does not mean a person is sick or will definitely become sick," said Dr. Elena Rostova, an occupational health specialist familiar with nuclear worker safety programs. "However, it does mean they need to be monitored. Beryllium sensitization can sit dormant for 20 or 30 years before turning into chronic lung disease."

Advocacy groups representing nuclear workers argue that the notifications are long overdue, pointing to long-standing issues with legacy contamination and air monitoring protocols at the 36-square-mile site.

"For years, workers have raised concerns about historical hot spots in older facilities that were never properly remediated," said a representative for a local labor union representing lab technicians. "We are glad the lab is finally coming clean, but for some former workers who are already sick, this information comes late."

### Safety oversights under scrutiny

This is not the first time Los Alamos has faced oversight questions regarding worker safety and environmental contamination. The laboratory has operated under intense scrutiny from federal watchdogs, including the Defense Nuclear Facilities Safety Board, over its handling of hazardous materials, radioactive waste, and safety culture.

The DOE established the Energy Employees Occupational Illness Compensation Program (EEOICP) decades ago to compensate workers who developed illnesses, including CBD, from exposure to toxic substances at federal nuclear sites. Officials confirmed that individuals receiving the notification letters will be eligible to file claims under the program if they test positive for beryllium sensitization or show signs of disease.

Lab officials emphasized that modern safety standards at the facility are significantly more stringent than in previous decades. Continuous air monitoring, advanced ventilation systems, and strict personal protective equipment (PPE) requirements are now standard in any area where beryllium is handled.

The lab has set up a dedicated hotline and medical assistance team to handle inquiries from concerned current and former staff. Officials have urged anyone who worked at or visited Los Alamos facilities and receives a notification to schedule a medical evaluation promptly.

Beryllium is a lightweight, high-strength metal prized by defense and aerospace contractors for its extreme thermal stability, rigidity, and resistance to corrosion. **LOS ALAMOS, N.M. (AP) — Oct. 22, 2008** — Officials at Los Alamos National Laboratory have begun notifying thousands of former workers about potential past exposure to trace amounts of beryllium, though lab authorities stressed Wednesday that the contamination was strictly surface-level and no illnesses have been reported.

The advisory letters are being sent to approximately 3,200 contractors and former employees who worked in select technical and administrative buildings at the nuclear research facility between 1998 and 2006. 

According to laboratory officials, routine environmental audits recently detected microscopic traces of beryllium dust on elevated surfaces, such as light fixtures and ductwork, in older facilities. Officials emphasized that the metal was confined to dormant surfaces and was not found suspended in the air.

"We are taking an abundance of caution in reaching out to our former workforce," said Kevin Roark, a spokesman for the laboratory. "The contamination identified was extremely low-grade and localized to surface dust. To date, we have zero reported cases of chronic beryllium disease or related symptoms linked to these specific areas."

Beryllium is a lightweight, high-strength metal historically used in defense manufacturing and nuclear weapons development. While harmless in solid form, inhaling microscopic particles or fumes can trigger Chronic Beryllium Disease (CBD), a severe lung condition, in individuals who have an allergic sensitivity to the element.

The notifications are part of a broader push by the U.S. Department of Energy to re-evaluate legacy facilities built during the Cold War. Following revised federal guidelines in the mid-2000s that drastically lowered the acceptable threshold for surface beryllium, sites across the national laboratory complex have been conducting updated sweep testing.

Lab officials said remediation teams have already cleaned and cleared the affected spaces. 

Former workers who receive the notification are being offered free medical consultations and blood tests through the Department of Energy’s Former Worker Medical Screening Program. 

"While the actual risk to individuals is believed to be exceptionally low, we believe providing full transparency and access to medical screening is the right course of action," Roark said.

The lab has established a toll-free hotline and a dedicated website for former personnel seeking more information about the screenings.
